related_questions.question: What should you do if you have high cholesterol?

text_blocks.snippet: To address high cholesterol, focus on lifestyle changes like dietary adjustments, increased physical activity, and quitting smoking, potentially alongside medication prescribed by a doctor. Specifically, reducing saturated and trans fats, increasing soluble fiber, and incorporating regular exercise can help improve cholesterol levels.
snippet_highlighted_words: focus on lifestyle changes like dietary adjustments, increased physical activity, and quitting smoking

list.title: Limit Saturated and Trans Fats:
list.snippet: Reduce intake of foods like fatty meats, processed meats, baked goods, and fried foods, which are high in saturated and trans fats, as these raise LDL (bad) cholesterol.

list.title: Increase Soluble Fiber:
list.snippet: Include foods like oats, beans, lentils, apples, and citrus fruits, as they help lower LDL cholesterol.

list.title: Incorporate Plant-Based Foods:
list.snippet: Increase consumption of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, which are naturally low in cholesterol and high in fiber.

list.title: Choose Healthy Fats:
list.snippet: Opt for unsaturated fats like olive oil, avocados, and nuts, which can help lower LDL cholesterol.

list.title: Consider Foods Fortified with Sterols and Stanols:
list.snippet: These plant-based compounds can help block the absorption of cholesterol.

list.title: Regular Physical Activity:
list.snippet: Aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise most days of the week.

list.title: Weight Management:
list.snippet: If overweight or obese, losing even a small amount of weight can improve cholesterol levels.

list.title: Statins:
list.snippet: If lifestyle changes are not enough, doctors may prescribe statins, which are the most common medications for lowering cholesterol by reducing the amount of cholesterol the liver makes.

list.title: Other Medications:
list.snippet: In some cases, other medications like ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitors may be used, according to some sources.

list.title: Quit Smoking:
list.snippet: Smoking damages blood vessels and increases the risk of heart disease, so quitting is crucial.

list.title: Limit Alcohol:
list.snippet: Excessive alcohol consumption can raise triglyceride levels and negatively impact cholesterol.

It's essential to consult with a healthcare professional to determine the best course of action based on your individual health status and risk factors. They can assess your cholesterol levels, discuss treatment options, and monitor your progress.

text_blocks.snippet: High cholesterol, specifically high levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, can lead to several serious health problems, most notably cardiovascular disease. This occurs because high LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of plaque in artery walls, a process called atherosclerosis. This plaque buildup can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart attack, stroke, and other circulatory issues.

list.title: Atherosclerosis:
list.snippet: High LDL cholesterol promotes the formation of plaque in arteries, which hardens and narrows the vessels. This process can affect arteries throughout the body, including those supplying the heart and brain.

list.title: Heart Attack:
list.snippet: When plaque ruptures, it can trigger the formation of a blood clot that blocks an artery supplying the heart muscle. This deprives the heart of oxygen and can lead to a heart attack.

list.title: Stroke:
list.snippet: Similar to heart attack, a stroke occurs when a blood clot blocks an artery supplying the brain, cutting off oxygen to brain tissue.

list.title: Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD):
list.snippet: PAD is a condition where plaque buildup restricts blood flow to the limbs, most commonly the legs and feet. This can cause pain, cramping, and even tissue damage.

list.title: Other Potential Problems:
list.snippet: High cholesterol can also contribute to conditions like chronic kidney disease and may increase the risk of certain inherited conditions, like familial hypercholesterolemia.

list.title: High Cholesterol Doesn't Always Cause Symptoms:
list.snippet: High cholesterol often doesn't cause noticeable symptoms until significant damage has already occurred. Regular blood tests are crucial for early detection.
